turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Wednesday, September 2. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — and we're starting at the Hague, where a five-judge panel just told India it has no choice but to honor a 66-year-old water treaty it very much doesn't want to honor.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled unanimously on Sunday that India must uphold the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty in full and curb construction on the Ratle hydro project on the Chenab River.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And India's response to a unanimous ruling was what, exactly?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Outright rejection — the Ministry of External Affairs says the court's jurisdiction itself is void, because India suspended the treaty back in April after the Pahalgam attack and doesn't recognize this panel's authority to rule on a treaty it's already walked away from. Pakistan's calling it vindication; New Delhi's calling it irrelevant.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So we've got a binding international ruling that one party has simply declared non-binding.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the real story — there's no enforcement mechanism here beyond reputational cost, and India's betting that cost is smaller than the cost of restoring water flows it's used as leverage since April. Watch whether Islamabad tries to escalate this at the UN, because a arbitration win with zero compliance is a test case for how much international law actually constrains a nuclear-armed state that's decided it doesn't care.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second — Germany just named a culprit for that cargo-airport drone strike from early August, and it's not who you'd guess from the headlines that week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Berlin's interior minister says Russian state agents directed the August 4th explosive-drone incident at the Leipzig-Halle cargo hub — and the response isn't a statement, it's expulsions. Germany's shutting Russia's Bonn consulate and its Berlin cultural center, and expelling staff tied to both.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A month gap between the incident and the accusation — what took so long?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's almost a month of forensic and signals-intelligence work before Berlin was willing to name a state actor on the record, which tells you they wanted this attribution airtight before taking a step this visible. Shuttering a consulate is a genuine downgrade in relations, not a symbolic slap — it's the kind of move that stays reversed for years, not months.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third — Washington's own institutional churn, this time at the top of the Army.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned Sunday after months of clashing with Defense Secretary Hegseth over the firing of Army Chief of Staff General Randy George and a string of other combat generals.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the Army's now missing both its civilian and military leadership at the same time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Correct — no Senate-confirmed civilian secretary, and the general Hegseth pushed out hasn't been replaced with anyone confirmed either. That's a genuinely unusual leadership vacuum at a service branch, and it's the clearest sign yet that Hegseth's purge of officers he sees as insufficiently aligned is producing real institutional cost, not just headlines.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto US business — the manufacturing data came in a little softer than expected.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: ISM's Manufacturing PMI printed 54.6% for August, against a 55.2% forecast and down from July's 55.6% — an eighth straight month of expansion, but New Orders fell to 53.7% from 56.7%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is an eighth straight expansion month still a positive story if the forward-looking piece is cooling that fast?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a real yellow flag, not a red one — New Orders is the subindex that leads the rest of the report, so a five-point drop there is the market's best early read that demand sentiment is softening even while current output holds up. Layer that against this week's jobs and CPI prints and you've got the Fed's own data run getting genuinely harder to read cleanly.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story — Broadcom reports after today's close, and the Street's expecting a very big number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Roughly $29.4 billion in revenue, up 84% year over year, and $3.22 in earnings per share, up over 90% — almost entirely AI-chip and infrastructure-software demand. This is the week's chip-sector bellwether, coming right behind Korea's export data and ahead of Nvidia's own print.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Internationally — Kazakhstan just created a job that didn't exist yesterday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: President Tokayev named his longtime adviser Erlan Karin, age 50, as the country's first-ever vice president, under a new constitution the Kurultai approved 141 to 4. Karin is now first in the line of succession.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does a Central Asian succession plan matter outside the region?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because Kazakhstan's been actively courting Western investment as a hedge against sitting entirely in Moscow's or Beijing's orbit, and a formalized, named successor removes exactly the kind of uncertainty that scares off long-horizon foreign capital. This is Astana signaling institutional continuity to investors, not just tidying up domestic politics.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one's a genuine surprise out of the Eurozone — inflation just jumped hard.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: August inflation came in at 3.3%, up from 2.9% in July, a three-year high, with energy inflation running at 14.3%. Markets are now fully pricing another 25 basis-point ECB hike, this time to 2.50%, at the September 10th meeting.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The ECB's already been hiking since that 2.25% move back in July — so this isn't a new direction, it's the cycle accelerating.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly right, and that's what makes it notable — the ECB was defending a single 25 basis-point move as sufficient just two months ago, and now inflation's already blown through that assumption and forced a second hike onto the calendar. Energy is doing most of the damage here too, which loops right back to the same oil story that's about to dominate our markets segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets — full board's on the app as always, and equities themselves aren't where the story is. S&P off 0.71%, Nasdaq down about a point, Dow off 0.78% — broad, unremarkable weakness, nothing near our threshold.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The number that did cross the threshold is oil. WTI jumped 5.9% to $90.82, Brent up 4.6% to $94.65 — and this is a fresh escalation, not a repeat of last week's Larak Island strike. A tanker was hit by an unidentified projectile off the Omani coast on Tuesday, fire extinguished, crew safe, investigation still open.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Fresh how — is this actually a new incident, or the same story getting recycled with a new headline?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely new — different location, different target type, and notably Qatar's Prime Minister is now flying to Tehran specifically to de-escalate, which wasn't happening after Larak. That's a real diplomatic response, not just another wire update on a war that's been running since February.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And gold didn't catch a safe-haven bid off any of this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the part I find most telling — gold actually fell 1.86%, because the Treasury story is currently stronger than the geopolitical one. Ten-year yields hit their highest level since January 2025 after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish remarks pushed September rate-hike odds to roughly 70%, and rising yields are simply beating out the safe-haven flow that would normally follow an oil-shock headline.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So which of those two forces, oil or rates, is actually going to matter more by Friday?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Rates, for my money — a single tanker incident is priced and re-priced within days, but a Fed chair signaling he's serious about a September move resets the entire curve, and that's before we even get to Friday's jobs report or CPI on the 11th. If oil keeps climbing into that data run, it does complicate the Fed's read, because a sustained Hormuz risk premium feeds straight into headline inflation right when policymakers are deciding whether August's cooling was real.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does that make Warsh more or less likely to soften his tone before the meeting?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Less likely, if anything — a hotter energy print gives him zero incentive to walk anything back, and markets know it, which is exactly why the ten-year kept climbing on a day equities were otherwise unremarkable. That's the whole segment in one line: watch yields and oil together this week, not the index board.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Alex, you sent me something this morning that has absolutely nothing to do with markets, power, or the AI buildout, and I want the full segment on it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a piece Adam Tooze flagged in Chartbook's Top Links this morning, built around a Wall Street Journal feature on what's happening to "moderately selective" private universities — and Syracuse is the case study.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Syracuse — sticker price north of $100,000, and it's in trouble?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the paradox. It's dropped seven straight years in the national rankings and just had its bond outlook cut to negative by S&P — while charging tuition that would suggest total pricing power. The mechanism is what makes this genuinely interesting.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Walk me through the mechanism.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Elite urban schools — NYU, Boston University, Northeastern — have converted location prestige into brutal selectivity, some down to 4% admit rates, with over 40% of their incoming classes paying full price. That lets them concentrate financial aid dollars on a much smaller admitted pool, which makes the aid go further per student and reinforces the prestige loop.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Syracuse can't do the same thing because it doesn't have the applicant volume to be that selective.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right — so it's forced to spread thinner aid dollars across a much wider admitted class just to fill seats, which is structurally the losing side of a winner-take-most dynamic. This is a moat story dressed up as a higher-ed story — selectivity itself has become the defensible asset, and everyone without it is fighting over margin in a shrinking pool.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this just Syracuse, or is the whole "moderately selective" tier exposed the same way?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The WSJ's framing — and Tooze's read on it — is that this is structural for the entire tier, not one school's mismanagement. There's a demographic enrollment cliff coming on top of it, US birth rates fell hard after 2008, so the applicant pool itself starts shrinking around 2026, which means the schools without a selectivity moat are about to be fighting over a smaller pie with a proven-worse hand.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually happens to a school like Syracuse if this doesn't turn around — realistically, not in the abstract?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The bond downgrade is the market's own answer to that question — negative outlook means credit-rating agencies think default risk is rising, which raises the cost of every future capital project, which makes it harder to invest your way out of the enrollment problem. It's the same credit-spiral logic you'd recognize from a subprime issuer, just wearing an ivy-covered building instead of a shopping mall.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: It's a genuinely different kind of story to end a headlines-heavy morning on, and I like that we went there.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly why it earned the full segment — sometimes the sharpest read on market structure isn't sitting in the AI-capex or energy data at all, it's sitting in a completely unrelated sector doing the exact same thing under a different name.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — and the biggest number in the inbox this morning came out of Seoul, not Washington.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Korea's committing $919 billion to a sovereign AI datacenter buildout — 8.4 gigawatts by 2029, 18.4 gigawatts by 2035. Phase one alone splits SK Group at 5 gigawatts, GS Group at 2.4, Naver at 1 — and SK Group is carrying the remaining 10 gigawatts of phase two essentially on its own.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely enormous commitment for one company inside one country's plan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: SemiAnalysis has already identified three active phase-one sites totaling 4.4 gigawatts under construction, so this isn't a paper announcement — steel's going in the ground now. And the offtake structure is the interesting part: not all of that sovereign-flagged capacity actually stays sovereign, a meaningful chunk gets sold to Anthropic and OpenAI as capacity, which gives Korea optionality to scale up national-model training later without stranding the buildout in the meantime.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's Nvidia's specific footprint inside all of that?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: SK Group's committed to 2 gigawatts of Rubin systems, Naver's separately signed for 200 megawatts, Samsung's building an Nvidia AI factory with over 50,000 GPUs, and SK Telecom's 2-gigawatt "DSX" AI factory is running Vera Rubin systems on SK Hynix's HBM4. SemiAnalysis believes Nvidia's locked in a long-term SOCAMM supply deal plus favorable HBM pricing and volume commitments with SK Hynix through 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why is Nvidia chasing a nation-state deal this hard instead of just selling more to the existing hyperscalers?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's commoditizing the complement at nation-state scale — several of Nvidia's biggest existing customers are also building competing custom chips, so diversifying the buyer base to include sovereign AI programs is a genuine hedge against concentration risk with its own largest customers. Korea's now the clear leader on this model, and the second-order read is watching which government copies the template next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story is a lot more procedural, but it's the kind of thing that changes how every future project gets built.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: MISO just formalized data-center load classification, becoming the third major grid operator to do it after PJM and ERCOT. The new filing splits "large loads" from "computational loads" specifically, defining the latter as large loads with at least 25 megawatts of IT-equipment demand.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does that split actually let MISO do that it couldn't do before?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Write requirements that target data centers specifically instead of lumping them in with any other large industrial customer — a steel mill and a hyperscale campus behave completely differently on the grid, and regulators finally have a formal category to treat them differently. This puts MISO on the same trajectory as PJM's ride-through scrutiny and ERCOT's large-load audit deadline in December — three of the country's biggest grid operators are now converging on the same conclusion independently.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that convergence good news for developers, or does it just mean more paperwork everywhere at once?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Both, honestly — more paperwork in the near term, because every RTO territory is about to have its own bespoke computational-load rulebook to navigate, but genuine long-term clarity once the rules settle, because right now developers are negotiating ad hoc against inconsistent standards in every territory. This is the regulatory precedent hyperscalers will be negotiating against everywhere else next.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Dalawang salita bago tayo pumunta sa Pilipinas, dahil pareho itong may kinalaman sa balita ngayon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Una, "kumupas." Ibig sabihin, humihina o nawawalan ng kulay, lakas, o halaga ang isang bagay — unti-unti, hindi biglaan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Paano ito naiiba sa "pagbagsak," na ginamit natin kahapon?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Malaking kaibahan iyan — ang "pagbagsak" ay biglaan at may bigat, tila isang malaking pagkabigo. Ang "kumupas" naman ay unti-unti, tulad ng kulay ng damit na dahan-dahang nawawala sa paglalantad sa araw — mahina ang timpla, hindi kaagad kapansin-pansin, pero patuloy na nangyayari.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya kapag ang piso ay "kumukupas," hindi ito biglaang pagbagsak kundi patuloy na paghina?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Eksakto — at iyon mismo ang salitang tama para sa sitwasyon ng piso ngayong araw, dahil apat na sunod na araw na itong humihina, hindi isang beses na malaking pagbagsak.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang pangalawa, "ikinukubli" — mula sa salitang-ugat na "kubli," ibig sabihin nakatago.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama — ang "ikinukubli" ay ibig sabihing sadyang itinatago ng isang tao o institusyon ang isang bagay mula sa iba, kadalasan may layuning maiwasan ang tanong o pagsisiyasat.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Paano ito naiiba sa payak na "itinatago"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "itinatago" ay puwedeng walang malisya — itinatago mo ang regalo bago ang kaarawan, halimbawa. Ang "ikinukubli" ay may bahid ng pagiging mahigpit at sadya, karaniwang may kaugnayan sa pananagutan o transparency na dapat sana ay hinihingi sa publiko.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kaya kapag sinabi nating "ikinukubli" ang isang bahagi ng badyet, malinaw na tayo ang tono — hindi ito neutral na paglalarawan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tama, at iyon mismo ang gagamitin natin sa susunod na segment, dahil parehong salita ito ang eksaktong wastong gamitin para sa balita ngayon.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Kumukupas na naman ang piso sa bagong pinakamababang antas — 62.565 kada dolyar ngayong Setyembre 2, ikaapat na sunod na record-low, mas mahina pa sa 62.40 kahapon.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang tunay na dahilan dito ay ang lakas ng dolyar mula sa pagtaas ng presyo ng langis at ang bagong tensyon sa Gitnang Silangan, hindi bagong hakbang mula sa BSP — kaya ito'y pagpapatuloy lamang ng kuwentong aming binanggit kahapon, hindi na naman bagong pagbabago sa patakaran.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English for the exact figures — the peso closed at 62.565 to the dollar Wednesday, an intraday low of 62.69, its fourth straight record-low close. This is dollar strength flowing through from the oil spike and the fresh Hormuz incident we covered in markets, not a new BSP action — the currency's now fading rather than crashing, which is exactly why we picked "kumupas" for it today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second story — and this one's a genuine legislative example of "ikinukubli." The Office of the President is asking Congress for 10.158 billion pesos for 2027, and 4.58 billion of that — nearly 45% — is confidential and intelligence expenses.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Almost half the budget is exempt from normal scrutiny by design.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the House committee waived detailed questions through what lawmakers called "parliamentary courtesy," fast-tracking approval with minimal debate. Representative Antonio Tinio of ACT Teachers publicly objected, calling it a "free pass," and pointedly tied his objection to the ongoing Duterte impeachment trial — the optics of concealing nearly half a presidential budget while impeachment testimony is actively probing confidential-fund abuse are not subtle.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Speaking of that trial — what happened today?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Day 21. Michael Poa, former DepEd chief of staff and defense spokesperson, took the stand and was immediately declared a hostile witness by presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero. Prosecutors also sought a subpoena to compel the PSA's Marizza Grande to testify.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A hostile-witness declaration on day one of someone's testimony is unusual — what does that actually signal?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It means the prosecution expected cooperation and got resistance almost immediately, which typically means Poa's account is going to conflict with what prosecutors believe the paper trail shows. It keeps this trial's core tension exactly where it's been for three weeks — confidential-fund accountability, playing out in real time against a budget request that's asking for more of exactly that kind of unaccountable spending.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last item — a genuinely awkward one for a sitting congressman.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Batangas Representative Leandro Leviste's company sold roughly 2.4 billion shares of SP New Energy Corp for about 3 billion pesos, cutting his stake to 11.51%, while Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla confirmed Leviste is under investigation for allegedly "selling" his solar franchise to Meralco's Pangilinan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Nothing on weather or the PSEi today?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No active PAGASA signal, and the PSEi just snapped a losing streak on ordinary bargain-hunting — nothing record-breaking, so both stay off the show. The peso and that budget number are where today's real story sits.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words tied to today's China story, and this pairing is genuinely useful for arguing about policy in general, not just this one story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First: 不然 — bùrán. It means "otherwise, if not" — a connective you use to state the consequence of NOT doing something.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: How's that different from 否则, which we've already taught?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 否则 is more formal, more 书面语 — you'd see it in a policy document or an editorial. 不然 is the everyday spoken equivalent, more 口语, the version you'd actually hear in a conversation or a briefing rather than read in a report. Same logical function, different register — knowing which one to reach for tells people something about how formal you're being. Example: 政府必须采取有效措施，不然房价还会继续下跌。"The government must take effective measures, otherwise home prices will keep falling."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second — 止跌企稳. That's a mouthful.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Zhǐ diē qǐ wěn — literally "stop the fall, seek stability." It's a set four-character policy collocation, very 书面语, and it's specifically the language Chinese officials use when describing the goal for a market that's been declining — not "grow," just "stop falling and stabilize."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So it's a deliberately modest goal, baked into the phrase itself.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly — the phrase itself signals the ambition level. Nobody uses 止跌企稳 to describe wanting a boom; you use it when the honest goal is just making the bleeding stop. Here's the sentence: 官方希望房价能尽快止跌企稳。"Officials hope home prices can stop falling and stabilize as soon as possible."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which is a perfect setup for exactly the story we're about to get into.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 尽管央行已经连续十五个月把利率维持在历史低位，房价仍然没有止跌企稳的迹象。In English — even though the central bank has held interest rates at record lows for fifteen straight months, home prices still show no sign of stopping their fall and stabilizing.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Give me the actual numbers, because "still falling" undersells how long this has been going on.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: New-home prices across 70 cities fell 0.18% month over month in July, worse than June's 0.15% drop — that's a 32nd consecutive month of decline. Urban fixed-asset investment is down 6.7% year to date through July, worse than the 5.7% figure at mid-year, and property investment specifically is down 19.2%. Only 17 of the 70 cities logged any monthly gain at all.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely long losing streak for rate cuts to have done nothing about.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which is the point — the one-year and five-year loan prime rates have sat frozen at 3.0% and 3.5% for fifteen months, and property prices simply haven't responded, because this isn't a rate problem anymore, it's a debt-deflation loop. Falling collateral values raise the real burden of developer and local-government debt even as nominal rates stay flat, and that dynamic doesn't reverse just because borrowing got cheaper.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And yet this is the same economy posting a genuinely enormous export number.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the two-speed story in one data set — July exports were up 23.9% year over year, with AI and high-tech shipments up more than 50%. You've got the tech and export side of the economy running hot at the exact same moment the property and investment side keeps deepening a debt-deflation hole rate policy hasn't touched.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: 不然的话，官方还能做什么？In English — if not that, what else can officials actually do?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the real open question — 不然 rate cuts, the toolkit left is mostly fiscal: more direct support for developers, or accepting a slower, managed deflation of the property sector while leaning entirely on exports and tech to carry growth. Beijing hasn't shown its hand on which path it's actually choosing yet, and that ambiguity is itself the story worth watching into the autumn.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts and culture — and we're opening with a sale that's really a restitution story wearing an auction-house label.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Christie's London will offer Kandinsky's 1907 painting "Das bunte Leben" — The Colorful Life — on October 14th, estimated above $30 million.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why is a Kandinsky sale the actual news, rather than just an auction listing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because of where it's been hanging — over 50 years at Munich's Lenbachhaus, on loan from a Bavarian bank, a provenance that looked entirely clean on the wall label. What that obscured is that the original owner, Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann, had sent the painting to Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum for safekeeping, and it was sold under duress in October 1940, months after the German invasion.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And that only came to light recently?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Germany's own Nazi-looted-art advisory commission ruled in 2023 that the 1940 sale bore every hallmark of forced dispossession, and the painting was restituted to her heirs after a six-year legal fight. It's now heading to market as a restituted work rather than a museum's quiet permanent loan — a case study in how much active provenance research is still reshaping blue-chip museum collections, in real time, decades after the fact.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second item's a fair, not a single work — Frieze Seoul's fifth edition and Kiaf Seoul's 25th opened together at COEX this week, running through the weekend.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The actual news is the new Spotlight section — it's revisiting 15 twentieth-century artists historically sidelined by a Western-centered art history, a genuine curatorial corrective, not just a sales gimmick.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is the market actually responding to that, or is it a nice curatorial footnote nobody's buying off of?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: ARTnews's on-the-ground read is that the real story this edition is a post-hype reckoning — after Seoul's meteoric 2022 boom, dealers are now actively testing whether Korean collector demand has genuine staying power once the novelty's worn off, and early sales reports are notably more measured than 2022's.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this edition is effectively a stress test for whether Seoul's boom was structural or just a moment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the read — if demand holds through this quieter, more sober edition, it validates Seoul as a durable fixture on the calendar rather than a 2022 flash. If dealers keep reporting soft sales through the weekend, expect the conversation to shift toward whether Asia's fair calendar overexpanded during the boom years.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two op-eds worth arguing with today, and they're both about who actually bears the cost of a fight nobody's formally declared over.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First — the Wall Street Journal's editorial board, "The Data Center Panic and U.S. Decline," published Sunday. Their argument is that the bipartisan backlash against data centers is mistaking symptom for disease — treating them as the villain behind rate hikes when abandoning the buildout doesn't lower demand for compute, it just hands the AI race to China, which the board argues won't be a benevolent hegemon if it wins.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where's the actual hole in that argument?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a false binary dressed up as strategic realism — nobody serious is proposing the US stop building data centers. What's actually being proposed, in real bipartisan PSC votes and utility rate cases, not just campaign ads, is that hyperscalers stop socializing grid and rate costs onto residential ratepayers. That's a market-design problem, not an anti-growth one, and the editorial conflates the two to make the backlash sound more irrational than it is.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece takes the same instinct — who pays for a strategic bet — and applies it to alliances instead of the grid.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Kurt Campbell and Rush Doshi in Foreign Affairs, "How Alliances Survive." Their argument is that US alliances won't just survive Trump-era strain, they could emerge stronger, because Russia-China convergence and deep economic entanglement are intensifying faster than any ally can actually hedge away from Washington. The real question, they argue, isn't survival — it's whether alliances evolve into "allied scale" platforms built to outmatch a combined China-Russia bloc.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a convenient conclusion for two people who used to run this exact policy.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the counter worth making — this reads like former Biden NSC officials grading their own homework, and "the architecture we built is too structurally necessary to fail" is precisely what you'd expect its own authors to conclude. It also glosses over that allies are actively diversifying right now — EU defense-autonomy pushes, Korea and Japan hedging with China trade — precisely because they no longer trust US policy continuity across administrations. Structural pull isn't the same thing as durable trust, and conflating the two is doing a lot of quiet work in that piece.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing to close, and it's a small sign outside a pizzeria that turned into something much bigger.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Daniel Romano runs D'Romano's Pizza in the Bronx. He saw a woman pulling a slice out of his trash can, sat her down, and fed her properly — then hung a handwritten sign out front telling anyone eating out of the garbage that he'd rather just give them a meal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What happened after the sign went up?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It went viral in late August, and strangers from around the country have since been calling the shop to pay for slices for people they'll never meet — paying it forward to someone hungry who might walk in that day.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's nothing to argue with in that story, no counter-take needed — someone saw a need directly in front of them and just met it, and it kept spreading on its own.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Wednesday, September 2. Have a good one — we'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Take care, everyone.
